title: The Verbal Arsenal
h1: 200+ Dominant Phrases — Because 'Be a Good Girl' Only Goes So Far
subhead: A complete phrase library organized by function — positioning, correction, praise, ownership, commands — plus the section on how you actually deliver them.
tagline: 200+ ready-to-use dominant phrases, organized by function — plus the delivery guide that makes them land.
meta_description: 200+ dominant phrases organized by function — positioning, correction, praise, ownership, commands. Plus the vocal delivery guide. Build your dominant voice.
problem:
You know what you want to say. You can feel the moment coming — the look, the shift in energy, the second where you're supposed to step in and say something that lands — and then your brain hands you absolutely nothing. Or worse, it hands you something generic, something you've heard in a movie, something that sounds correct but feels hollow the second it leaves your mouth.

Dominant presence isn't just what you say. But the words are load-bearing. And if you freeze when it matters, the moment dies.

This is the fix.
inside: 200+ ready-to-use phrases — real lines, organized so you can find them when you need them
Positioning phrases — how to establish authority at the start of a scene or interaction
Correction phrases — what to say when behavior needs redirecting, without escalating or undermining
Praise phrases — the specific language of 'good girl' that actually works vs. the kind that feels patronizing
Ownership language — possessive, claiming, framing phrases that make a submissive feel held
Transition commands — how to move from ordinary time to scene without an awkward gear change
The delivery section — tone, pace, vocal presence. Because a dominant phrase delivered in a confused tone is just a confused sentence
who_for: You go quiet in scenes when you should be speaking — not because you don't know what you want, but because the words won't come
You have a vocabulary of about four dominant phrases and you're tired of rotating through them
You're newer to dominance and you want to hear how this is supposed to sound before you try to build your own voice
who_not: If you're looking for complete scene scripts, start with one of the three Tension Scene Collection volumes. The Arsenal is a reference library, not a scene guide
If you're already fluent and confident with dominant language — you probably already have most of these

faq.q: Won't using someone else's phrases feel fake?
faq.a: Not if you use them the right way. You don't have to read from the list in the moment — you read the list, absorb what resonates, practice it until it becomes yours. Every actor learns other people's lines. Every musician learns other people's songs. That's how you develop a voice.

Mostly yes — it's written from the dominant perspective. That said, a lot of submissives read it to understand what good dominant communication sounds like, and occasionally to wish very hard that their partner had read it.

faq.q: Does the delivery section get into voice training or is it more conceptual?
faq.a: It's practical, not theoretical. Specific guidance on pace, register, volume, silence. Not 'project authority' but 'speak slower than feels natural, pause before the key word, don't rise at the end of a command as though it's a question.' That level of specific.
